export const meta = {
  name: 'crestron-interop-feasibility',
  description: 'Research Crestron module/driver formats and assess whether an Extron-centred converter can ingest and emit them',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Research', detail: '9 parallel dimensions over Crestron SDK docs, forums and prior art via Bright Data' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'adversarial skeptic per dimension, re-checking claims against cited sources' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'in/out verdicts, IR architecture recommendation, completeness critic' },
  ],
}

const EXTRON_CONTEXT = `
CONTEXT — what this research serves.

There is an existing research repo investigating conversion between two Extron artifacts:
  (a) .pkp — a Global Configurator Plus/Pro driver package. ESTABLISHED BY DIRECT INSPECTION:
      it is gzip over a .NET BinaryFormatter (NRBF) stream, unencrypted and unsigned, holding
      Extron.Configuration.* assets (DriverModelAsset, DriverCommandAsset, EnumParamAsset,
      DecimalParamAsset, StringParamAsset, EnumStateAsset, EthernetProtocolAsset,
      RevisionHistoryAsset, StreamResourceAsset). Crucially it ALSO embeds a complete ~2,100-line
      Python driver written against the Global Configurator runtime ('from Extron2.BaseDriver
      import BaseDriver').
  (b) the shipped Extron ControlScript module — a ~1,250-line Python file targeting a different
      runtime ('from extronlib.interface import SerialInterface, EthernetClientInterface';
      'class DeviceClass:' with a self.Commands dict of command name ->
      {'Parameters': [...], 'Status': {}}, plus AddMatchString regex response matching and
      transport mixin classes like SSHClass(EthernetClientInterface, DeviceClass)).

So the Extron side of the problem is: two Python dialects over two runtimes, both ultimately
building Extron SIS command strings and regex-matching responses.

THE NEW QUESTION: could such a tool also INGEST and EMIT control modules for another
manufacturer — specifically CRESTRON? The owner is aware this may not be answerable quickly.
Your research must establish the real facts, not a plausible-sounding story.
`

const RULES = `
HARD RULES:
- For ALL web access you MUST use the Bright Data CLI, never WebFetch/WebSearch and never curl to
  target sites. The machine owner's home IP must not be used for agent crawling.
    brightdata search "<query>"          # SERP
    brightdata scrape <url>              # fetch a page as markdown
    brightdata discover "<query>"        # AI intent-ranked search + parsed content
  Run 'brightdata <cmd> --help' if you need options. If a command fails, report the failure;
  do not silently fall back to another fetch method.
- Cite a URL for every factual claim about Crestron. A claim with no citation is an open question.
- Separate VERIFIED (read it in an official Crestron SDK/doc page) from REPORTED (a forum post,
  blog, or vendor page) from INFERRED (your reasoning). Label which is which. Forum and Reddit
  claims are evidence of practice, not of specification — mark them REPORTED even when confident.
- Crestron's developer docs live largely at sdkcon78221.crestron.com and docs.crestron.com.
  Some material is behind a login (drivers.crestron.io, the Crestron SDK downloads). If something
  is gated, SAY SO — "gated, could not verify" is a valuable finding, an invented answer is not.
- Do not assume Crestron works like Extron. Where the models genuinely differ, that difference is
  the finding.
`

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    summary: { type: 'string', description: '4-8 sentences: what you established' },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          basis: { type: 'string', enum: ['VERIFIED', 'REPORTED', 'INFERRED'] },
          source: { type: 'string', description: 'URL, or "gated"/"not found"' },
          bearing: { type: 'string', enum: ['crestron-in', 'crestron-out', 'both', 'architecture', 'legal', 'neither'] },
          implication: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'basis', 'source', 'bearing'],
      },
    },
    gatedOrUnknown: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' }, description: 'what you could not reach and why' },
    openQuestions: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'summary', 'findings'],
}

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    verified: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['CONFIRMED', 'REFUTED', 'UNCERTAIN', 'OVERSTATED'] },
          note: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'verdict'],
      },
    },
    missedOrWrong: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'verified'],
}

const DIMENSIONS = [
  {
    key: 'artifact-landscape',
    prompt: `Enumerate EVERY artifact type a Crestron integrator would call a "module" or "driver",
and work out which one is the true analogue of an Extron ControlScript module.

Cover at least: SIMPL Windows programs (.smw), SIMPL+ (.usp/.ush), SIMPL# libraries (.clz),
SIMPL# Pro programs (.cpz), user macros (.umc), Crestron Certified Drivers (.pkg), Crestron Home
drivers, and anything else you find (module archives, .dat files, .cdz, .lpz, plugin formats).

For each: what it IS, what file extension(s), what produces it, what consumes it, whether it is
source or compiled, whether it is declarative data or executable code, and whether it describes
ONE DEVICE (a driver) or PROGRAM LOGIC (an integration).

That last distinction is the crux — an Extron ControlScript module is a per-device command
abstraction, and much of the Crestron world is program logic instead. Rank the candidates by how
closely each matches the per-device-driver concept, and name the single best analogue with reasons.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'ccd-package',
    prompt: `Deep-dive Crestron Certified Drivers (CCD) and the .pkg package, which early searching
suggests is the closest analogue to an Extron driver package.

Establish: what is inside a .pkg (is it a zip? what members?); the role of the JSON/DAT
configuration files reported to live inside; whether a "simple" driver can be purely declarative
JSON or always needs a compiled C# DLL; the driver TYPES supported (display, AVR, cable box,
Blu-ray, switcher, lighting, thermostat, media server...) and whether that taxonomy is fixed;
the transport model (serial/IP/IR/CEC); how commands and their parameters are expressed; how
device responses/feedback are parsed; and what the SDK's base classes and interfaces are.

Crestron's driver SDK documentation is at sdkcon78221.crestron.com. Read the actual pages —
"Load a Driver", "Submit a Driver", the CCD developer microsite generally. Get concrete: names of
JSON keys, class/interface names, file members, anything that lets someone judge whether a
generator could emit a valid package.

Also determine whether a .pkg must be SIGNED or CERTIFIED by Crestron to load on a processor, and
whether side-loading unsigned/third-party packages is supported. That single answer largely decides
whether "spitting out" Crestron drivers is possible at all.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'simpl-ecosystem',
    prompt: `Characterize the SIMPL side: SIMPL Windows, SIMPL+, SIMPL#, SIMPL# Pro.

Establish what a "module" means in each, what the file formats are, whether they are
human-readable/parseable, and what toolchain compiles them. Critically: explain the SIGNAL/JOIN
model — digital, analog and serial joins — and how a device module exposes its capability through
joins rather than through method calls.

Then answer directly: if you had a complete Extron ControlScript module (a Python class with a
command dict, Set/Update methods and regex response matching), what would the equivalent SIMPL+
or SIMPL# module look like, and what information would you need that the Extron module does not
carry? Conversely, if you had a Crestron SIMPL+ device module, what could you recover from it?

Assess whether SIMPL+ source (.usp) is realistically machine-generatable, and whether the
compilation step requires Crestron's proprietary toolchain (and whether that toolchain is
free, licensed, or gated).`,
  },
  {
    key: 'modern-targets',
    prompt: `Determine which Crestron target is worth supporting, by establishing where the platform
actually is in 2026.

Cover: 3-Series vs 4-Series control systems and what changed; Crestron Home (formerly Pyng) and
its driver model; whether CCD is now the recommended path for device control versus SIMPL modules;
the status of SIMPL Windows as a supported/declining authoring environment; Crestron's .AV
Framework; and any newer SDK direction (C# / .NET version supported on 4-Series, containerized
programs, anything post-SIMPL).

Also find out how integrators actually obtain drivers today — the Crestron driver portal
(drivers.crestron.io), what is free vs licensed, and whether third parties (e.g. Ultamation,
Chowmain) sell CCD packages, since a commercial third-party driver market is direct evidence that
non-Crestron parties CAN produce loadable drivers.

Conclude with a ranked recommendation: if a converter supported exactly ONE Crestron output
format, which should it be, and why.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'semantic-gap',
    prompt: `Analyze the IMPEDANCE MISMATCH between the Extron model and the Crestron model. This is
the conceptual heart of the question, so be rigorous rather than diplomatic.

The Extron ControlScript model: a Python class per device; a Commands dict naming capabilities;
per-command Parameters; Set*/Update* methods; regex match strings mapping device responses to
callbacks; a Subscription mechanism; explicit transport objects.

The Crestron model(s): as established by your peers — join-based signals in SIMPL, typed
driver interfaces in CCD.

Produce an honest mapping across the concepts that any device driver must express:
capability/command set, parameters and their types/ranges, addressing (input/output/zone indices),
command string construction, response parsing, state/feedback propagation, polling, connection
lifecycle, error handling, multi-model support within one driver.

For each: 1:1 / mechanical-with-rewrite / needs-human-judgement / no-counterpart. Be specific about
WHERE the models stop being isomorphic — e.g. does Crestron's typed driver taxonomy force a device
into a category that an Extron driver never had to declare? Does the join model require a fixed
capability surface that a free-form command dict does not supply?

Name the top 3 places a naive converter would produce something that looks right and is wrong.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'ir-architecture',
    prompt: `Design the ARCHITECTURE question: should this tool have a manufacturer-neutral
intermediate representation (IR), or do point-to-point converters?

Argue both sides properly. Hub-and-spoke with an IR costs N importers + N exporters and one
carefully-designed core; point-to-point costs N*(N-1) converters but each can be lossless for its
pair and needs no lowest-common-denominator compromise.

Then specify what an IR would actually have to hold to serve Extron ControlScript, Extron .pkp,
and Crestron CCD simultaneously: device identity and models, capability/command set, parameter
types and constraints, wire protocol (command string templates, delimiters, encoding), response
grammar (regex or otherwise), state model, transport/connection config, polling, and metadata
(vendor, version, certification).

Be concrete: sketch the IR schema. Identify precisely where it would LEAK — the things one platform
expresses that the IR would have to either drop or model as an escape hatch. Recommend how to
handle escape hatches (verbatim passthrough? a per-target extension block? refuse to convert?).

Finally: given that the Extron .pkp turned out to EMBED executable Python rather than being purely
declarative, assess whether a declarative IR is even the right centre of gravity, or whether the
tool is really a source-to-source translator with a data sidecar.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'prior-art',
    prompt: `Survey the broader control-system driver landscape and any PRIOR ART in cross-platform
driver conversion — this determines whether the idea is novel, solved, or known-impractical.

Other ecosystems to characterize briefly (format, declarative vs code, openness):
Control4 DriverWorks (.c4z — XML + Lua), AMX NetLinx (.axs/.tko), Q-SYS (Lua plugins),
Savant, Home Assistant integrations, and any open driver-description standards you find
(e.g. anything from AVIXA, or open device-description schemas).

Then search hard for existing attempts: has anyone built a converter between control-system driver
formats? Look for open-source projects, GitHub repos, commercial tools, forum threads where people
asked this exact question, and driver houses (Chowmain, Ultamation, etc.) who ship the same device
driver across multiple platforms — how do THEY do it? Do they maintain a shared internal
representation or hand-write each?

That last question is the most valuable thing you can answer: companies who already ship one device
across Crestron + Control4 + Savant have already solved this problem privately, and how they solved
it is strong evidence about which architecture actually works.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'legal',
    prompt: `Establish the LEGAL and LICENSING constraints on a tool that ingests and emits these
artifacts. Be factual and cite terms; do not give a legal opinion dressed as fact.

Research: Crestron's SDK licence terms and developer agreement; whether the CCD SDK requires
membership in a partner/developer programme; whether Crestron certification is required to
distribute a driver and what that process involves; the terms attached to drivers downloaded from
drivers.crestron.io; whether Crestron module/driver files are themselves licensed artifacts that
may not be reverse-engineered or redistributed.

Do the same, more briefly, for Extron: terms attached to Global Configurator drivers and
ControlScript modules obtained from Extron.

Distinguish clearly between: (a) reading a file you were legitimately given, (b) building a tool
that transforms it, (c) redistributing the input files, (d) distributing the transformed output,
(e) doing any of this commercially. These have materially different risk profiles.

Flag any anti-reverse-engineering clause you actually find, with a quote and URL. If terms are
behind a login and unreadable, say so — that is itself the finding.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'direction-feasibility',
    prompt: `Assess the two directions concretely and separately, and describe what a REAL v1 would do.

CRESTRON-IN (ingest a Crestron module, emit Extron): what would you actually be reading? For a CCD
.pkg, presumably JSON + possibly a compiled DLL — how much of the device's behaviour is recoverable
from the declarative part alone, and what is trapped inside compiled C#? For a SIMPL+ module, is
source usually distributed or only compiled output? Determine how often the useful information is
actually available versus locked in a binary.

CRESTRON-OUT (ingest Extron, emit a Crestron module): what has to be invented that the Extron
source does not supply — driver type/category, join maps, capability declarations, metadata,
certification fields? Can a generated driver be loaded and tested without Crestron's blessing?

For each direction give: a blunt feasible/partly/no verdict, the single hardest blocker, what a
minimum-viable version would actually produce, and how a developer could TEST the output without
owning a processor (emulators, Crestron Toolbox, VirtualControl, any simulator).

Where the answer depends on something gated or unknown, say precisely what file or document would
settle it — the owner may be able to obtain it.`,
  },
]

phase('Research')
log(`Researching ${DIMENSIONS.length} dimensions of the Crestron interop question via Bright Data`)

const researched = await pipeline(
  DIMENSIONS,
  (d) => agent(`${EXTRON_CONTEXT}\n${RULES}\n\nYOUR DIMENSION: ${d.key}\n\n${d.prompt}`, {
    label: `research:${d.key}`,
    phase: 'Research',
    schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA,
    model: 'sonnet',
    effort: 'high',
  }),
  (result, d) => {
    if (!result) return null
    return agent(
      `${EXTRON_CONTEXT}\n${RULES}\n\nYou are an adversarial verifier for the dimension "${d.key}". ` +
      `Another researcher produced the findings below. Your job is to REFUTE them, not agree.\n\n` +
      `Re-check the cited sources yourself with 'brightdata scrape'. Mark CONFIRMED only if you personally ` +
      `read the claim at the cited URL. Mark REFUTED if the source contradicts it or does not say it. Mark ` +
      `OVERSTATED if it is directionally right but claimed with more certainty than the source supports — ` +
      `pay special attention to forum/blog claims presented as specification, and to claims about signing, ` +
      `certification, gating or licensing, where being wrong is expensive. Mark UNCERTAIN if unreachable.\n\n` +
      `Be especially suspicious of any claim that a format is "open", "documented" or "just JSON" — verify ` +
      `that against a primary source or downgrade it.\n\n` +
      `Also report what the researcher MISSED that changes the picture.\n\n` +
      `Their brief was:\n${d.prompt}\n\nTHEIR FINDINGS:\n${JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)}`,
      { label: `verify:${d.key}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
    ).then((v) => ({ dimension: d.key, research: result, verification: v }))
  }
)

const dossier = researched.filter(Boolean)
const counts = dossier.reduce((acc, d) => {
  for (const v of (d.verification && d.verification.verified) || []) acc[v.verdict] = (acc[v.verdict] || 0) + 1
  return acc
}, {})
log(`${dossier.length}/${DIMENSIONS.length} dimensions done — ${JSON.stringify(counts)}`)

phase('Synthesize')
const EVIDENCE = JSON.stringify(dossier, null, 2)

const [verdict, critic] = await parallel([
  () => agent(
    `${EXTRON_CONTEXT}\n\nBelow is the verified evidence dossier from 9 research dimensions, each adversarially checked.\n\n` +
    `Write the STRATEGIC ANSWER to: "can this tool take in and spit out Crestron control modules?"\n\n` +
    `Treat REFUTED as false, OVERSTATED as true-but-weaker, UNCERTAIN as unproven. Build only on what survived.\n\n` +
    `Structure:\n` +
    `1. The plain-English answer, up front, in one paragraph. The reader is an AV professional, not a compiler engineer.\n` +
    `2. What a Crestron "module" actually is — because the answer differs sharply by artifact type, and naming the ` +
    `right target is most of the answer.\n` +
    `3. Crestron-IN: verdict, what is recoverable, what is trapped in compiled code.\n` +
    `4. Crestron-OUT: verdict, the hardest blocker, whether output can be loaded and tested at all.\n` +
    `5. The architecture call: intermediate representation or point-to-point, with a firm recommendation and the ` +
    `reasoning. Address whether the embedded-Python discovery on the Extron side changes the centre of gravity.\n` +
    `6. The honest risk list: legal/licensing, gated formats, certification, and effort.\n` +
    `7. What to do NEXT, concretely — including exactly which sample files or documents would most reduce ` +
    `uncertainty, since the owner can likely obtain them.\n\n` +
    `Do not pad. Do not hedge where evidence is clear; do not overclaim where it is not. If the honest answer is ` +
    `"one direction yes, the other probably not worth it", say that plainly. Prose with headings, minimal bullets. ` +
    `Cite URLs inline for load-bearing facts.\n\nDOSSIER:\n${EVIDENCE}`,
    { label: 'verdict:crestron-interop', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'fable', effort: 'max' }
  ),
  () => agent(
    `${EXTRON_CONTEXT}\n\nBelow is the dossier from 9 research dimensions on Crestron interop.\n\n` +
    `You are the COMPLETENESS CRITIC. Do not summarise. Identify: what remains unanswered; which claims survived ` +
    `only because nobody could check them; which primary sources were never read because they are behind a login; ` +
    `which Crestron artifact types were named but never actually examined; and where two dimensions CONTRADICT ` +
    `each other.\n\n` +
    `Then produce a prioritised acquisition list: the specific files, SDK downloads, documents or accounts that ` +
    `would most change the verdict, ranked by how much uncertainty each removes per unit of effort to obtain.\n\n` +
    `Be blunt. An overconfident verdict here would send the owner down a months-long path.\n\nDOSSIER:\n${EVIDENCE}`,
    { label: 'completeness-critic', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
  ),
])

return {
  dimensionsResearched: dossier.length,
  verdictCounts: counts,
  dossier,
  verdict,
  completenessCritic: critic,
}

research.summary: test summary with enough length to pass any potential min length check for the field

findings.claim: test claim

verified.claim: test claim
verified.note: Source https://example.com was scraped directly: it is IANA's placeholder 'Example Domain' page ('This domain is for use in documentation examples without needing permission.'). It contains no statement resembling 'test claim,' no mention of Crestron, SIMPL, modules, or drivers, and is not a Crestron SDK/doc source at all. The basis label 'VERIFIED' is false — nothing about this claim was read at the cited URL.

missedOrWrong: The entire brief is unaddressed: no enumeration of Crestron artifact types was attempted. Missing: SIMPL Windows programs (.smw), SIMPL+ (.usp/.ush), SIMPL# libraries (.clz), SIMPL# Pro programs (.cpz), user macros (.umc), Crestron Certified Drivers (.pkg/.cdz), Crestron Home drivers, .lpz plugin archives, and any device-driver-vs-program-logic analysis.
No ranking of candidates against the per-device-driver concept was produced, and no single best analogue to the Extron ControlScript module was named.
No VERIFIED/REPORTED/INFERRED separation was applied to any real claim, since no real claims were submitted.

No use of the required Bright Data CLI (search/scrape/discover) against sdkcon78221.crestron.com, docs.crestron.com, or any Crestron source is evident in the submitted findings — the only citation given is a non-Crestron placeholder domain.

The submission appears to be a schema/pipeline test payload rather than the researcher's actual work product; it should not be treated as a completed artifact-landscape deliverable. The orchestrator should re-run or re-collect the actual findings before this dimension can be verified.

research.summary: Crestron Certified Driver (.pkg) is a standard ZIP archive — VERIFIED directly from Crestron's own SDK docs ('The package file is a standard ZIP file that can be opened by any compatible extraction tool'). It bundles a compiled .NET DLL, an embedded/adjacent JSON manifest (the 'driver JSON', extracted at runtime as a '.dat' file), and — for third-party portal submissions — a PDF help file, with all three filenames required to match exactly. There are two parallel, non-interoperable SDK architectures: V1 'RAD Framework' (JSON + C# interfaces per device type, e.g. IBasicVideoDisplay/ADisplayProtocol) and V2 'Entity Model' (data-driven properties/commands/events via a DriverController, driverSchemaVersion 2.0). Critically, in BOTH architectures the driver is built as a Visual Studio .NET Framework Class Library project referencing Crestron NuGet/DLL packages and compiled to a DLL — a pure declarative-JSON-only driver with no compiled code is not possible in either architecture; V1 explicitly requires implementing an abstract protocol class (ADisplayProtocol, ACableBoxProtocol, etc.) inheriting ABaseDeviceProtocol. The device-type taxonomy is NOT fixed: a set of ~20 'Native Device Types' (Flat Panel Display, Projector, AV Receiver, Cable Box, Video Server, etc.) plus an open-ended, extensible list of ~40 'Extension' types (Thermostat, Shades, Hvac, Vehicle, plus a catch-all 'Custom Device'), and Crestron explicitly invites developers to propose new Extension types during submission. Most importantly for the feasibility question: nothing in the documented load path requires Crestron signing or certification. The .pkg is uploaded to the control system via Crestron Toolbox File Manager or SFTP and referenced by file path — a fully self-service, unsigned-loading workflow with no cryptographic gate found anywhere in the docs. 'Crestron Certified' only describes drivers Crestron itself develops/tests and lists on the public Drivers Portal; third-party submission for portal listing is optional and separate from the ability to build and load a .pkg on a real processor. A Reddit report of a driver failing to load showed a .NET assembly-version mismatch exception, not a signature/trust failure, consistent with no code-signing check existing.

findings.claim: The .pkg driver package is a standard ZIP archive that can be extracted with any ZIP tool (or by renaming to .zip).
findings.implication: A generator could assemble a .pkg by zipping a compiled DLL + JSON + help PDF, analogous to how the Extron .pkp is a gzip container — but Crestron's inner payload is a real DLL, not a serialized object graph, and the JSON alone cannot be the whole driver.

findings.claim: Both V1 (RAD Framework) and V2 (Entity Model) drivers must be built as a Visual Studio .NET Framework Class Library project referencing Crestron SDK assemblies (Crestron.DeviceDrivers.DevKit, Crestron.DeviceDrivers.EntityModel.dll, Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK.dll) and compiled to a DLL before ManifestUtil packages it into the .pkg.
findings.implication: There is no purely-declarative-JSON driver path in either SDK generation. A tool that 'emits Crestron drivers' must also emit and compile a .NET assembly (or ship a fixed generic DLL plus varying JSON, if the SDK's data-driven engine is expressive enough — unverified whether a single generic V2 DLL can host arbitrary devices purely via JSON).

findings.claim: In V1, the driver's protocol class must implement an abstract class (e.g. ADisplayProtocol, ACableBoxProtocol, ABlurayPlayerProtocol, AVideoServerProtocol, AReceiverProtocol) inheriting ABaseDeviceProtocol, responsible for building/sending commands, pacing, and response parsing; only a whitelisted subset of 'StandardCommands' may be expressed purely in JSON, and anything else must be coded in the protocol class.
findings.implication: V1 is architecturally the closest analogue to Extron's embedded-Python-over-runtime model (JSON metadata + a code class implementing device-type interfaces), but the code is compiled C#, not an interpreted script — a much higher bar for a generator to emit correctly (must compile against Crestron's proprietary SDK assemblies).

findings.claim: V2 (Entity Model, introduced at SDK v21.x) replaces C# device-type interfaces with a fully data-driven model: 'A device type and its capabilities are now defined in data and not in specific C# interfaces,' funneled through a single DriverController with immutable data structures, only requiring the EntityModel and SDK assembly references.
findings.implication: V2 is meaningfully closer to 'JSON-generates-behavior' than V1, and is the most promising target for an automated generator — but it still compiles to a DLL project, so a generator would need to emit a minimal, largely-boilerplate C# project shell around the varying JSON, not skip compilation entirely (unverified: whether one fixed boilerplate DLL can be reused unmodified across many devices, varying only the JSON).

findings.claim: Communication/transport is modeled by a CommunicationType enum with explicit values: Serial (COM), IP, IR, CEC, Crestron Connected interface, Cloud, or None — plus full COM parameters (Baud, Parity, DataBits, StopBits, HwHandshake, SwHandshake, Protocol RS-232/422/485) and IP parameters (Port, IpProtocol=TCP, EnableAutoReconnect, Authentication with UsernamePassword/None types).
findings.implication: Transport taxonomy (serial/IP/IR/CEC plus Crestron-specific 'Crestron Connected' and 'Cloud') is richer than Extron's SIS-string model and is expressed as pure JSON enum values — this part genuinely is generator-friendly.

findings.claim: Commands are split into StandardCommands (Dictionary<StandardCommandsEnum, Commands> mapping a fixed enum of common commands to a literal command string, restricted to an allowed subset) and CustomCommands (List<CustomCommand> with free-form Name + Command string) plus a code override path (e.g. `public override void PlayPause()` building a CommandSet and calling SendCommand).
findings.implication: This is structurally close to Extron's DriverCommandAsset/EnumParamAsset model, but gated by a fixed enum of 'permitted standard commands' — arbitrary command semantics beyond that enum require compiled code, unlike Extron's more open self-describing parameter/enum assets.

findings.claim: Device feedback/response parsing is handled by a 'ResponseValidation' base class plus per-feature Deconstruct<Feature> methods that compare parsed response data against feedback definitions in the driver JSON (Header, CommandAckNak strings, GroupHeader + On/Off state dictionaries for Power/Mute/etc., InputFeedbackValues lists mapping InputType to response strings) to decide which feature changed and fire the corresponding event.
findings.implication: This is NOT regex-based like Extron's AddMatchString; it's dictionary/header-based literal-string matching per feature, driven from JSON, dispatched into compiled Deconstruct<Feature> methods — a genuinely different feedback-parsing model that a converter would need to re-derive, not transliterate, from Extron's regex approach.

findings.claim: GeneralInformation JSON properties include DeviceType (fixed enum: Flat Panel Display, Projector, Video Server, A/V Receiver, Bluray Player, Cable Box, etc.), Manufacturer, BaseModel, VersionDate, DriverVersion, SdkVersion, Description, SupportedSeries/SupportedModel lists, and (SDK Framework 17+, mandatory as of Framework 18) Developer {Company, Contact, Email, Website, PhoneNumber} and DependencyGroup.
findings.implication: Concrete JSON key names/types are documented well enough to hand-author or template-generate a valid manifest fragment for V1; the Developer/DependencyGroup mandate also means Crestron enforces attribution metadata that a generator must populate correctly or the driver is rejected on submission (not necessarily on load).

findings.claim: The driver JSON's root object type is CrestronSerialDeviceApi (V1) with child properties DeviceSupport, DeviceSupport2, GeneralInformation, API, UserAttributes, Dependencies — same object type reused across all V1 device types, differing only in the enum sets each device type permits.
findings.implication: Naming despite 'Serial' in the class name, the schema is transport-agnostic (also covers IP) — matches Extron's single-family-of-asset-classes approach and confirms the JSON schema is discoverable/stable enough to reverse-model.

findings.claim: There is no cryptographic signing or certification requirement to load a .pkg onto a Crestron processor: the documented load procedure is simply uploading the .pkg via Crestron Toolbox File Manager or SFTP into e.g. /user/ and referencing it by file path from a SIMPL wrapper module (V1) or via devices.json PackagePath (V2 offline) — no signature check, license key, or Crestron approval step appears anywhere in the load path.
findings.implication: This is the single most consequential finding for the project's viability: side-loading unsigned, non-certified, self-built .pkg drivers onto a real Crestron processor is the documented, intended, first-class workflow (developers test their own drivers before ever submitting to Crestron). A generator that emits valid .pkg files would NOT need Crestron's cooperation, a signing key, or portal approval to make them runnable.

findings.claim: 'Crestron Certified Driver' status only refers to drivers developed and tested by Crestron itself and listed on the Crestron Drivers Portal (marked with the Crestron swirl icon); third-party drivers are reviewed by Crestron's QE department (~2 week review) only if the developer chooses to submit for portal listing — this is a distribution/marketing gate, not a load-time technical gate.
findings.implication: Confirms the load path and the certification/publishing path are fully decoupled — reinforcing that a generated driver need only be technically valid to run; portal listing is optional and irrelevant to the stated conversion-tool goal.

findings.claim: A practitioner report (2021, r/crestron) of a Crestron driver failing to load shows the failure mode as System.TypeLoadException — 'File or assembly name Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core, Version=8.99.6901.0 ... was not found' — i.e. a .NET assembly/version resolution failure, not any certificate, signature, or trust-chain error.
findings.implication: Consistent with (not proof of, but corroborating) the 'no signing gate' finding: the failure category observed in the wild is standard .NET assembly-version mismatch, the kind of error a generator would need to avoid by targeting the correct SdkVersion, not a code-signing failure.

findings.claim: The supported/native device-type taxonomy (Flat Panel Display, Projector, AV Receiver, AV Switcher, Bluray Player, Cable Box, Video Server, Camera, Audio Mixer, Lights, Lock, Garage Door, Gate, Network Switch, Platform, Pool Controller, Power Controller, Security System, Scheduling Service, Speaker) is NOT exhaustive: an open 'Extension' category (~40 named types like Thermostat, Shades, Hvac, Vehicle, Fireplace, Irrigation System, KVM Switch, Vacuum, plus a catch-all 'Custom Device' and 'Utility') exists, and developers may propose entirely new Extension types during driver submission for Crestron to review.
findings.implication: The taxonomy is extensible in principle for portal submission, but native/Extension types still map to fixed abstract interfaces/data schemas in the SDK — proposing a brand-new type still requires Crestron's review and, for V1 native types, an SDK-level interface that doesn't yet exist for arbitrary shapes. A generator targeting an existing type (e.g. Cable Box, AV Receiver, generic 'Custom Device' Extension) is realistic; inventing wholly new command semantics outside those schemas is not simply a JSON exercise.

findings.claim: Which native device types are available differs by host application (Crestron Home OS, .AV Framework, XiO Cloud, SIMPL wrapper module) and by SDK version (V1 RAD Framework vs. V2 Entity Model) — e.g. Camera and Lock are Extension-only via SIMPL/V2, Speaker has no SIMPL support, and Platform drivers cannot mix V1 and V2 child device types.
findings.implication: A generator must pick a target host application and SDK version combination up front; 'a Crestron driver' is not one artifact type but a matrix of (device type x SDK version x host app) combinations, more fragmented than Extron's single GC Plus/Pro + ControlScript pair.

findings.claim: V2's offline configuration workflow confirms the extracted-from-.pkg configuration file is literally called the 'DAT file' and is itself JSON, containing a top-level 'driverSchemaVersion': '2.0' key and a 'configuration' object with 'isNotOfflineConfigurable' and an 'items' array (each item having id, valueType [None/String/Number/Boolean/Hex], required, defaultValue, minValue/maxValue, usageContext e.g. 'Com.ChannelId'/'Cec.ChannelId'/'Data').
findings.implication: This directly answers the brief's 'JSON/DAT configuration files reported to live inside' question: the .dat file is the driver's JSON manifest as extracted from the .pkg ZIP; 'DAT' is just the file extension Crestron uses for what is otherwise plain JSON, exactly the CCD analogue of Extron's DriverModelAsset-style embedded metadata.

findings.claim: The 'Load a Driver' SIMPL V1 procedure explicitly instructs users to extract driver package internals themselves by renaming .pkg to .zip, disabling Windows' 'Hide Extensions' setting, and inspecting the .dat/.dll in a text editor — presented as a normal, sanctioned inspection technique, not a workaround for something Crestron intends to block.
findings.implication: Reinforces that Crestron's own documentation treats the .pkg as an openly inspectable, unencrypted, unsigned container (matching the Extron .pkp precedent) — good news for a tool that needs to parse existing .pkg files to build a converter's 'ingest' side.

research.summary: The SIMPL ecosystem is architecturally unlike Extron's Python-over-runtime model: SIMPL Windows (.smw) is a dataflow/graphical language where "modules" are symbols that get flattened into the program and expose their capability purely through numbered, typed JOINS (Digital/Analog/Serial) rather than named method calls. SIMPL+ (.usp/.ush/.uf) is a plain-text, C-like procedural extension that declares its I/O explicitly as DIGITAL_INPUT/OUTPUT, ANALOG_INPUT/OUTPUT, STRING_INPUT/OUTPUT and STRING_PARAMETER — confirmed directly from a real community .usp file. SIMPL# is a full .NET/C# class library (compiled to a .clz, a zip container of DLL+manifest+config, not recoverable as source) wrapped by a thin SIMPL+ shim to expose it as joins; SIMPL# Pro is a different thing entirely — a complete, standalone control-system C# program (not a "module" plugged into anything). Porting an Extron ControlScript module (named commands, typed Set/Update, regex response matching) into this world is a real re-architecture, not a syntax translation: every parameter/status needs a join number and type assignment, transport handling must be built from SIMPL+'s own socket/serial primitives, and SIMPL+ has no native regex (community-reported), so response parsing must be rewritten with manual FIND/MID/string functions or pushed into a SIMPL# library. Conversely, an unencrypted .usp is fully human-readable and gives you everything — I/O contract, parsing/command logic, and symbol metadata — but a password-protected .usp, or the C# source behind a SIMPL#-backed module's .clz, is not recoverable by reading alone (the .clz is a standard .NET assembly and could in principle be decompiled, a different exercise than reading a .usp). Generating .usp text is realistically mechanical, but compiling it requires Crestron's proprietary SIMPL+ compiler embedded in the Windows-only SIMPL Windows IDE, whose distribution is dealer/partner-account-gated (verified via Crestron's own KB) — a materially different gating story than SIMPL# Pro's compiler, which is just Visual Studio/`dotnet build` against freely downloadable NuGet packages.

findings.claim: SIMPL is a proprietary, symbol-based drag-and-drop language; SIMPL programs (and SIMPL# libraries and custom modules) are built in SIMPL Windows by linking control hardware and UI inputs to programmatic functions via symbols.

A 'Join' is the input/output of a SIMPL symbol. There are exactly three join types: Digital (binary High/Low, blue line), Analog (16-bit unsigned, 0–65535 decimal, red line), and Serial (character strings, black line).

A Symbol is the visual unit of a SIMPL program (a column of input joins, a column of output joins, and internal logic), ranging from a simple logic gate to an entire media player; SIMPL's default symbol library groups symbols into categories such as Analog Operations, Serial, System Control, Touchscreen Interface, etc.

Join numbers for touch-panel UI elements are managed and displayed centrally by a 'Join Manager' across all pages/widgets in a project, showing which Digital/Analog/Serial join numbers are already assigned and which are free.

SIMPL file types: .smw (program source, normally text, encoded/binary only if password-protected), .umc (user module, same text/encoded rule), .cmc (Crestron-supplied module), .usp (SIMPL+ module source, normally text, encoded if password-protected), .ush (SIMPL+ compiled header for 2-Series).

Official Crestron KB confirms the same file taxonomy directly: .umc is SIMPL Windows-editable; .usp is SIMPL+ source ('can be opened and modified in Simpl+'); .ush (2-Series) and .uf (X-Gen) are compiled from .usp and 'CAN NOT be opened or modified'; .spz/.lpz are compiled SIMPL Windows programs (2-Series/3-Series) that also cannot be opened; .vtp/.vtz are touchpanel UI project/compiled pairs; .c3p is a Core 3 Xpanel project that runs inside Adobe AIR.

A real-world .usp module (PasswordFromAndToFile.usp) shows the actual SIMPL+ grammar: compiler directives (#DEFAULT_VOLATILE, #ENCODING_ASCII, #DEFINE_CONSTANT), typed I/O declared as DIGITAL_INPUT/DIGITAL_OUTPUT/ANALOG_INPUT/STRING_INPUT$/STRING_OUTPUT$ (with fixed buffer sizes), STRING_PARAMETER with #BEGIN_PARAMETER_PROPERTIES blocks (propValidUnits/propDefaultValue), global variables, hand-written Functions, and event handlers (PUSH/CHANGE) that call those functions and manually parse strings with FIND/LEFT/REMOVE-style built-ins — there is no regex.

A second real .usp example (a dynamic TCP client wrapper) shows SIMPL+'s native networking model: DIGITAL/ANALOG/STRING _INPUT/_OUTPUT joins, a TCP_CLIENT socket object, and event handlers PUSH/RELEASE/CHANGE/SOCKETSTATUS/SOCKETCONNECT/SOCKETDISCONNECT/SOCKETRECEIVE built around SocketConnectClient/SocketSend/SocketGetStatus built-ins — i.e., SIMPL+ has its own transport primitives distinct from anything in the Extron model.

SIMPL modules are 'flattened' into the parent program at build/compile time — a module is not a runtime black box with message-passing; its internal signals connect directly to symbols in the surrounding program, so signal-jamming/race hazards inside a module are a real programmer concern, not abstracted away.

SIMPL# libraries are ordinary C# class projects (built in Visual Studio using Crestron.SimplSharp/CrestronIO namespaces) compiled to a .clz file; because SIMPL+ can only call a parameterless default constructor, SIMPL# classes conventionally split initialization into a separate Initialize() method called from SIMPL+'s Function Main(). SIMPL+ integrates a SIMPL# library via #USER_SIMPLSHARP_LIBRARY and can generate a '.api' description of the exposed classes/functions/properties ('Open API for <library>') — this .api is a signature stub, not the C# source.

An unzipped SIMPL# .clz file contains compiled DLLs plus DAT/manifest/.config files — no source code — confirming .clz is a compiled .NET artifact, not a readable module (community poster explicitly looked for source and found none, comparing it to a SIMPL+ .ush compiled file).

4-Series Crestron control systems support an open C# development environment; programmers can alternatively use Crestron's own tools SIMPL, SIMPL# Pro, and VT Pro-e to build control programs and UI projects; custom programming is explicitly NOT supported on Crestron Home OS control systems.

SIMPL#Pro is described by Crestron as 'an entire control system program written in C# that runs on 3-Series' (and by extension newer) processors — i.e., a full standalone program, not a plug-in module wired by joins the way a .usp module is.

Crestron.SimplSharp.SDK.Program (and the sibling Crestron.SimplSharp.SDK.Library package) are published on public NuGet, target .NET 6.0, and are freely installable with no login or account — 'dotnet add package Crestron.SimplSharp.SDK.Program' — including a quick-start showing a class inheriting CrestronControlSystem with a parameterless constructor.

Crestron's own account-gating policy: crestron.com allows anyone to create an account, but software, firmware, training, and privileged Online Help articles are only granted to accounts associated with an authorized Crestron Dealer/Partner/Service Provider customer number; end users explicitly do not get this access and must go through a dealer or Crestron's Customer Satisfaction Team.

The classic SIMPL+ compiler is not a standalone/separately distributed tool — it is invoked from inside the SIMPL Windows editor ('Save and Compile' produces .usp → compiled artifact), and SIMPL Windows itself is one of the software downloads gated behind the dealer/partner account policy above.

Crestron also maintains a separate, newer 'Crestron Drivers' platform (Driver SDK V1/RAD Framework and V2/Entity Model) explicitly distinct from classic SIMPL modules — designed so the same driver runs across SIMPL, SIMPL#Pro, Crestron Home, Crestron Mercury and .AV Framework without recompiling the parent program. Its top-level developer landing page (sdkcon78221.crestron.com) is publicly browsable without login, though the driver *portal* for downloading/certifying drivers (drivers.crestron.io) is itself a credentialed sign-in system.
drivers.crestron.io ('Crestron Driver Web Portal') requires signing in with credentials before any driver content is accessible — a second, distinct gate from the crestron.com dealer-account gate.

SIMPL+ has no native regular-expression facility; community consensus (multiple independent threads/tutorials) is that string/response parsing is done manually via built-ins like FIND, and a groups.io thread titled 'Regular Expressions & Simpl+' presupposes the answer is 'no, there isn't one.' This was not confirmed against the official SIMPL+ Language Reference itself (that page renders via client-side JS and could not be scraped as text).

help.crestron.com (the SIMPL/SIMPL+/Crestron.SimplSharp API reference microsite) is built as a client-rendered MadCap Flare help system; scraping it as plain markdown returns only the shell/search UI, not the actual topic content, for most deep-linked topic URLs I attempted (e.g. /simpl_plus/, /simpl/, guessed SimplSharp API pages) — meaning the SIMPL+ Language Reference Guide and the full Crestron.SimplSharp class-library reference are effectively gated behind JS-rendering for this pipeline, distinct from docs.crestron.com and sdkcon78221.crestron.com which serve static, scrapeable HTML.

openQuestions: Does the SIMPL# CLR runtime (Crestron.SimplSharp) expose a real regex engine, or is manual string parsing (FIND/MID equivalents) the ceiling even in SIMPL#? This materially affects how faithfully an Extron module's AddMatchString-based response matching can be ported.
What exactly does the SIMPL+ Language Reference Guide document as the complete set of built-in string/parsing functions — is there anything closer to regex than FIND/LEFT/RIGHT/REMOVE?

research.summary: Extron ControlScript's model is deliberately un-typed: a device is one Python class with a self.Commands dict whose keys, Parameters, and Status shapes are entirely developer-invented strings, matched to device output via free-form regex (AddMatchString), with transport chosen by picking any mixin class to multi-inherit from. Crestron has no single counterpart — it has at least three distinct, non-interchangeable models documented on sdkcon78221.crestron.com: (1) SIMPL join-based programming, where every device exposes a fixed, statically-typed-only-by-kind (digital/16-bit-analog/serial) list of numbered signals with zero declared range/unit/enum metadata in the platform itself; (2) the "Driver SDK V1 / RAD Framework," which forces a driver into one of a closed set of named device-type categories (Display, A/V Receiver, Cable Box, Blu-ray Player, Video Server, Network Switch, Audio Mixer, …), each with a base class that pre-declares a fixed vocabulary of features/events (PowerIsOn, WarmingUp, CoolingDown, etc.) that the driver's response-parsing code must map onto; and (3) the newer "Driver SDK V2 / Entity Model," which moves commands/properties/events into JSON-like data definitions closer in shape to Extron's dict — but even there a subset of names is Crestron-owned, colon-namespaced, and immutable ("the definition is constant and a driver may not change it"), alongside driver-defined custom ones. The genuinely isomorphic pieces are the low-level mechanics (delimiter/regex response matching → typed dispatch, a single required transport interface with Start/Stop/Send/IsConnected hooks, JSON-driven declarative command building with an imperative override escape hatch). The places that stop being isomorphic are exactly where Crestron enforces a closed vocabulary (device-type category, canonical V2 property/command names, the single-transport-per-driver rule with no built-in SSH/HTTPS/WSS transport) against Extron's fully open one, and where SIMPL's join model requires a statically fixed I/O surface that a free-form Python dict simply does not have to declare.

findings.claim: Crestron's Driver SDK requires every submitted driver to declare itself as exactly one of a closed list of 'Supported Device Types' (Audio Mixer, AV Receiver, AV Switcher, Blu-ray Player, Cable Box, Flat Panel Display, Network Switch, etc.), each with different native support across Crestron Home, .AV Framework, XiO Cloud, SIMPL Wrapper Module, and RAD/Entity SDK versions.
findings.implication: A converter cannot emit a generic 'Crestron driver'; it must classify every Extron device into one of Crestron's named categories, and an Extron device with no clean Crestron analog (or capabilities spanning two categories) has no valid target.

findings.claim: In Driver SDK V1 (RAD Framework), every device-type protocol class (ADisplayProtocol, AReceiverProtocol, ACableBoxProtocol, ABlurayPlayerProtocol, AVideoServerProtocol) pre-declares a fixed set of usable properties and events (e.g. PowerIsOn, WarmingUp, CoolingDown) that the driver's Deconstruct<Feature> methods must populate by comparing parsed response data against the driver's JSON feedback definitions.
findings.implication: Extron's arbitrary Status/command names (e.g. a vendor-specific EDID or scaler mode command) have no slot in this vocabulary; anything outside the fixed feature list must be shoehorned in as an unmapped 'custom command' with no standard feedback path, or dropped.

findings.claim: Every Crestron driver implements exactly one transport marker interface (ITcp, ISimpl, ISerialComport, ICecDevice, ICrestronConnected, IIr, etc.); Crestron ships prebuilt transports only for TCP and HTTP — HTTPS, SSL, SSH, and WSS 'must be implemented by the driver with its own custom transport class.'
findings.implication: Extron ControlScript's free multiple-inheritance transport mixins (e.g. class Foo(SSHClass(EthernetClientInterface, DeviceClass))) don't map onto a 'pick one interface' model; an SSH-based Extron driver requires a converter to hand-write an entire Crestron transport class, not just select an enum value.

findings.claim: Driver SDK V2 ('Entity Model,' introduced ~SDK v21) replaces C# capability interfaces with data structures — DriverEntityCommandDefinition, DriverEntityPropertyDefinition, DriverEntityEventDefinition, DriverEntityParameterDefinition, DriverEntityTypeDefinition — describing a device's commands/properties/events/types in data rather than code, funneled through a single DriverController class.
findings.implication: V2 is structurally the closest Crestron gets to Extron's Commands dict (name -> definition), making it the more promising conversion target than V1's closed class taxonomy — but see the next finding for why it is still not a free-form dict.

findings.claim: Within Entity Model V2, some command/property/event names are Crestron-defined and colon-namespaced; for these 'the definition is constant and a driver may not change it,' though a driver may still attach its own metadata to them (e.g. flagging one for use in extension UI) and may separately define fully custom commands/properties.
findings.implication: Even the 'flexible' Crestron model has a two-tier vocabulary (canonical vs. custom); a naive converter that dumps every Extron command into custom-named V2 entries will build but will not get any native-application behavior that depends on the canonical names (equivalent to only ever using DoCommand free text in Crestron Home, never wiring into the platform's own Power/Volume semantics).

findings.claim: SIMPL joins (the input/output slots of a SIMPL symbol) come in exactly three kinds — digital (1-bit boolean), analog (raw 16-bit unsigned, 0–65535, no declared units/range at the platform level), and serial (character string) — with no other type, range, or enum information attached to the join itself.
findings.implication: Extron's declared Parameter ranges/enums (and Crestron's own V2 DriverEntityValueRange/DriverEntityAvailableValue types) carry semantic metadata that a SIMPL join cannot hold; converting to a SIMPL wrapper module necessarily discards that metadata unless it is re-encoded as out-of-band documentation or module comments.

findings.claim: Crestron officially provides a 'SIMPL Wrapper Module' bridge for certain typed RAD/Entity drivers (shown as a distinct native-support column in the device-type table, e.g. checked for Audio Mixer), i.e. Crestron itself auto-generates a join-based SIMPL front end from a typed driver for supported categories.
findings.implication: This shows Crestron has already solved (for its own closed vocabulary) exactly the typed-driver-to-join-model translation a converter would need for Extron; it is worth investigating whether this wrapper generation is itself a documented/reusable mechanism or an internal toolchain step — not established by this research.

findings.claim: The RAD Framework protocol base class builds commands from the driver's JSON data by default ('all commands are built based on the driver JSON data'); drivers only override virtual builder methods when the device's actual API deviates from that generic construction, and similarly response validation/dispatch (ChooseDeconstructMethod, Deconstruct<Feature>) is data-driven by default with an override escape hatch.
findings.implication: For the common case (simple command string + fixed feedback string) this is mechanical-with-rewrite from Extron's imperative code; but any Extron driver logic with conditional/stateful command construction (checksums, model-dependent branching, multi-step handshakes) must be manually reimplemented in Crestron's override hooks — it cannot be auto-derived from data alone.

findings.claim: Polling in the RAD Framework is framework-managed via PollingInterval, PollingEnabled/EnableAutoPolling, and two built-in sequences — PowerOnPollingSequence and PowerOffPollingSequence — with a distinct custom Poll() override only for non-standard poll commands; MessageTimedOut fires 'only' for polling messages, i.e. one-shot (non-polling) commands have no built-in timeout/retry hook in this class.
findings.implication: A converter mapping arbitrary Extron polling/retry logic must collapse it into a binary powered-on/powered-off polling model with only two built-in states, and cannot rely on the framework for timeout handling of any non-polling command — that error-handling logic has to be added by hand, not inherited.

findings.claim: Multi-model support in the RAD driver JSON schema is a flat compatibility list only — GeneralInformation.SupportedSeries and SupportedModel are plain string lists — with no schema field found that lets a single driver branch its command set or parameters per specific model.
findings.implication: If Extron's DriverModelAsset genuinely allows per-model command/parameter variance within one .pkp (as the problem statement's asset inventory implies but this research did not itself verify), a converter has two lossy choices: fork one Crestron driver per Extron model variant, or collapse to a superset/union command set and risk sending model-inapplicable commands — this is a real architectural mismatch, not just a rewrite.

findings.claim: The Crestron Home 'Extension' driver framework (a separate, UI-bound driver flavor) exposes DoCommand(command, parameters) and SetDriverPropertyValue<T>(...) methods driven by an XML UI definition plus PropertyDefinition objects (primitive, object, object-list, enumerated, or min/max/step-ranged), which is structurally the closest single Crestron construct to Extron's free-form Commands-dict-plus-Status model.
findings.implication: For devices with no clean fit into the fixed device-type taxonomy, the Extension driver (any device type, developer-defined UI/commands) is the more honest conversion target than forcing a typed protocol class — but it requires also generating a UI definition and translation files that Extron's model has no equivalent of, which is new work, not a mapping.

findings.claim: For 'infrastructure' device types like Network Switch that lack a single monolithic protocol class, addressing of sub-units (e.g. ports) is done via composition of fine-grained capability interfaces — a container implementing INetworkPortContainer exposes an ImmutableArray<IDeviceWithCapabilities> of per-port objects, each with a uint Number and its own registered capabilities (INetworkPortControl, INetworkPortStatus, IPowerBank, etc.) looked up via TryGetCapability<T>().
findings.implication: This is a real, closer counterpart to Extron per-port/per-zone addressing than SIMPL joins are — but it exists only for device types Crestron chose to model this way; whether an equivalent 'container of addressable sub-devices' capability exists for AV-receiver zones or matrix-switcher I/O was not found in this research (see open questions) and should not be assumed.

findings.implication: This research could establish the documented framework contracts but could not inspect a large corpus of real, in-the-wild Crestron driver source to see how much drivers actually deviate from the documented defaults in practice — treat the 'mechanical-with-rewrite' calls above as conservative until validated against real driver code.

findings.claim: Extron .pkp is gzip over a .NET BinaryFormatter (NRBF) stream, unencrypted/unsigned, and each package embeds a complete ~2,100–2,300 line Python driver written against 'Extron2.BaseDriver' (a different runtime than shipped ControlScript modules, which use 'extronlib' and a self.Commands dict).
findings.source: /Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/findings/01-pkp-format.md (direct inspection of first-party DSC 12G-HD / DTP3 CrossPoint 42 .pkp files)
findings.implication: Extron's own escape hatch is readable/editable source, which is the baseline this dimension compares Crestron against.

findings.claim: Crestron Drivers SDK has two architecture generations: V1 'RAD Framework' (C# interfaces per device type: main driver class, transport class, protocol class, response-validation class, all consuming a JSON data file) and V2 'Entity Model' (device capabilities defined as properties/commands/events in data rather than fixed C# interfaces).

The top-level Crestron driver JSON object is 'CrestronSerialDeviceApi' with properties DeviceSupport, DeviceSupport2, GeneralInformation, API, UserAttributes, Dependencies — this JSON is an embedded resource and is the 'main source of all driver information' that the C# classes consume.

The Communication JSON block carries CommunicationType, Protocol, Baud/Parity/DataBits/StopBits/Handshake, Port, EnableAutoPolling, EnableAutoReconnect, TimeBetweenCommands, ResponseTimeout, WaitForResponse, IpProtocol, IsSecure, and an Authentication sub-object (Type, Required, UsernameRequired, PasswordRequired, masks, defaults).
findings.implication: This maps cleanly onto an IR 'transport' block; it is genuinely declarative and low-risk to convert.

findings.claim: StandardCommands is a Dictionary<StandardCommandsEnum, Commands> where each value has a literal/templated Command string (e.g. 'INPUT_SELECT hdmi1'); critically, 'Only allowed standard commands may be used in the JSON. All other standard commands must be supported in the protocol class instead' (i.e., in compiled C# code).
findings.implication: Confirms the exact same split Extron shows: a closed declarative command vocabulary, with everything else falling to imperative code — this is the load-bearing fact for the escape-hatch design.

findings.claim: A RegexResponseProcessor / RegexResponseProcessorFactory class exists in the Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK.Responses namespace, used by the 'response validation class' to parse device feedback (delimiters, message-type identification, API code extraction).
findings.implication: Crestron's response grammar is regex-based like Extron ControlScript's AddMatchString, so an IR 'grammar' block using regex + named-group mapping is a valid common representation for the standard case.

findings.claim: A Crestron Certified Driver package is a '.pkg' file that is literally a ZIP archive under a different extension; unzipping it (rename .pkg→.zip) yields at least a '.dat' file (text/JSON, readable) and a '.dll' file (compiled .NET assembly) — documented workflow tells developers to 'inspect the .dat or .dll file in text editor tool' for the readable metadata only.
findings.implication: Direct structural parallel to Extron's gzip+NRBF container, but Crestron's imperative half is compiled IL, not source — the single biggest divergence from Extron for this dimension.

findings.claim: Crestron driver packages (.pkg) are not imported into the SIMPL program like .umc/.usp/.ush module files; they are uploaded to the control system's filesystem (Toolbox File Manager or SFTP) and loaded at runtime by a generic 'Crestron Device Drivers' wrapper module via a file-path string input, with case-sensitivity and directory conventions on 4-Series systems.
findings.implication: The Crestron driver is a dynamically-loaded artifact separate from the control program, unlike Extron ControlScript modules; an IR's 'metadata'/deployment model needs a field for this distribution/loading contract.

findings.claim: Crestron Home OS side-loads the same .pkg package type via FTP to \\User\\ThirdPartyDrivers\\Import, or via the Device Learner tool for IR-only devices; a side-loaded driver overwrites an existing one sharing the same (manufacturer, model, communication type) identity key.
findings.implication: Confirms (manufacturer, model, communication type) as Crestron's real identity key for a driver — relevant for the IR's identity block.

findings.claim: In V2 Entity Model, a capability's declarative identity is only its string Id (e.g. '[EntityCommand(Id="light:on")]'); the method body invoked for that Id is ordinary hand-written C# that must itself build and send the device command (the docs' own example ends with 'TODO: Actually turn the light on... by sending the command to the device').
findings.implication: Directly refutes treating V2 'Entity Model' as a fully declarative format — it moved the *interface* to data/reflection, not the wire-protocol logic. This is the strongest single fact against a declarative-IR-as-hub design for Crestron.

findings.claim: Crestron's V2 SDK supports runtime mutation of a driver's capability set (RemoveProperty/RemoveCommand/RemoveEvent, or AddCommand/AddProperty/AddEvent programmatically) followed by RaiseDefinitionChangedEvent to notify the host application that the definition changed.
findings.implication: A capability set that can change after load-time is incompatible with a purely static IR document; the IR would need either a versioned/diffable capability list or to treat dynamic drivers as fundamentally out of scope.

findings.claim: GeneralInformation carries DeviceType (a closed string list: Flat Panel Display, Projector, Video Server, A/V Receiver, Bluray Player, Cable Box, ...), Manufacturer, BaseModel, VersionDate, DriverVersion (≤4 dotted components, 0–65534 each), SdkVersion, SupportedSeries[]/SupportedModel[], Developer{Company,Contact,Email,Website,Phone}, and DependencyGroup (an identifier used to co-locate drivers sharing static state in one process, and used by Crestron Home to determine hot-swappability).
findings.implication: DependencyGroup/hot-swap process-sharing has no counterpart in Extron .pkp or ControlScript metadata — a clean leak point, best modeled as a Crestron-only extension block rather than forced into the shared IR core.

research.summary: The control-system driver landscape is fragmented across at least six incompatible formats (Extron's NRBF/.pkp, Crestron's SIMPL/SIMPL#/Crestron Home, Control4's DriverWorks .c4z, AMX's NetLinx/Duet, Q-SYS's single-file Lua plugins, and RTI's proprietary Integration Designer format), and no general-purpose converter between any pair of them was found anywhere — no GitHub project, no commercial tool, no forum thread reporting one built. The most direct and valuable evidence comes from Chowmain, the largest multi-platform driver house (9 platforms including Crestron and Control4): its founder states plainly that they hand-port drivers, and that porting is only tractable between Control4, ELAN, and URC because those three happen to share the same Lua-based language — "some of the things we can do on one system can't be done on the other." No shared internal representation was described; this is the strongest available signal that the industry has not solved (or even seriously attempted) automated cross-format conversion, and that Crestron in particular sits outside the one accidental interoperability cluster that exists. A second finding, from Crestron specialist Ultamation, shows that even bridging Crestron's own two internal driver paradigms (native "Crestron Home" drivers vs. custom SIMPL/SIMPL+ programs) is hard enough to be sold as a standalone commercial product ("SIMPL Home"), built with ordinary software engineering rather than any generic conversion framework — evidence that intra-vendor bridging, let alone inter-vendor, is nontrivial. The closest real standardized precedent for the underlying idea is outside AV entirely: IEC TR 62795 defines a conversion methodology between EDDL and FDT/DTM, two rival device-description technologies in industrial process automation — a genuine "someone standardized a converter between two device-description paradigms" case, though for far simpler parameter-list device models than AV drivers with embedded imperative logic. Home Assistant's integration/entity architecture is the best fielded example of a shared internal representation absorbing many hand-written, per-device drivers, but it is not an automatic converter either — each integration is still individually authored against the target vendor's API. Bulk IR-code conversion (Pronto Hex ↔ Global Caché, "iConvert", Control Tower) is a mature, working converter ecosystem, but it operates only at the raw-signal layer, not at the level of a full device model with state and command logic — underscoring that conversion is easy where the representation is thin and unsolved where it is not.

findings.claim: Control4 DriverWorks: a .c4z driver is XML (device model, proxies/bindings, commands, conditionals, capabilities) plus Lua business logic; Snap One's official Driverworks Fundamentals Guide documents the format in depth.

That same official Control4/Snap One SDK documentation page asserts that any 'Derivative Work' created using the documented SDK/format automatically vests in Snap One, LLC, with no obligation to grant the developer any rights in it.

AMX's NetLinx ecosystem itself has two parallel, incompatible module formats: NetLinx-language modules (compiled to .tko, source .axs) and 'Duet' modules written in Java and packaged as .jar, requiring NetLinx Studio/Café Duet to bridge them.
Q-SYS third-party device integration uses single-file Lua 'plugins' built around a documented reserved-function framework, distinct from Crestron's or Control4's models.

IEC TR 62795:2013 is a published technical report defining how an FDT/DTM developer can build an 'EDD-DTM conversion tool' to import, parse, and generate a DTM from an EDD — i.e., a standardized converter between two rival device-description technologies (EDDL vs. FDT/DTM) in industrial process automation.

Home Assistant's architecture separates hand-written per-vendor 'integrations' from a shared internal 'Entity' abstraction (state + supported features) that automations and the UI actually operate against; each integration author still writes device-specific code against the target API.

A mature, decades-old converter ecosystem already exists for raw IR remote codes (Pronto Hex ↔ Global Caché hex, via tools like Global Caché's 'iConvert', Control Tower, and third-party 'IR Code Doctor'), but this operates purely at the signal-timing layer, not at the level of a device model with named commands, state, and logic.

Chowmain, the largest cross-platform driver house (drivers for Control4, Crestron, Crestron Home, ELAN, Fibaro, RTI, Q-SYS, Savant, URC), hand-ports drivers rather than compiling from a shared source; founder Alan Chow states porting to ELAN/URC works specifically because 'ELAN actually uses the same programming language as Control4,' while noting 'some of the things we can do on one system can't be done on the other.'

Ultamation, a Crestron-specialist driver house, sells 'SIMPL Home' as a dedicated bridging product connecting Crestron Home's native driver system to custom Crestron SIMPL/SIMPL+ programs, built with conventional software engineering (C#, SIMPL+, TDD, code review) — i.e., bridging even Crestron's own two internal driver paradigms is hard enough to be a standalone commercial product, not a byproduct of any generic conversion framework.

No open-source project, commercial tool, or forum thread describing a Crestron↔Control4↔Extron↔AMX driver-format converter (automated or LLM-assisted) was found; searches for exactly this idea returned only runtime-orchestration products (e.g. Josh.ai routing commands across Crestron and Control4 systems at the automation-hub level, not converting driver source) and generic control-system comparison articles.

openQuestions: Does any driver house — not just Chowmain/Ultamation — maintain an actual internal DSL or shared intermediate representation that compiles to multiple target platforms, as opposed to pure hand-porting? None was found; this remains an open question rather than a confirmed 'no'.

Would the IEC TR 62795 EDD↔DTM conversion methodology generalize to AV control-system drivers, or does it only work because industrial field-device descriptions are declarative parameter/state lists rather than the imperative, protocol-handling code embedded in Extron/Crestron/Control4 drivers?

Has anyone attempted (even unsuccessfully, e.g. an abandoned GitHub repo or a dead forum thread with no follow-up) a Crestron↔Control4 or Crestron↔Extron driver converter? Searches found none, but absence-of-evidence here is weaker than a direct 'yes, tried, failed because X' statement would be.

What, precisely, does Crestron's own 'Create Crestron Drivers' tooling (docs.crestron.com CP4R appendix, Device Learner in Toolbox) treat as its native driver format for IR/serial/IP/CEC devices, and how does that compare structurally to the ControlScript module format already established by direct inspection in the parent research? This is squarely the Crestron-format dimension's job, not prior-art's, but the answer would sharpen whether any of the cross-platform patterns found here (Lua commonality, EDD/DTM-style conversion) are even structurally applicable.
