# Can this tool take in and spit out Crestron control modules?

Basis note: of the nine dossier dimensions, three (artifact-landscape, modern-targets, direction-feasibility) came back as placeholder stubs and one (simpl-ecosystem) was never adversarially checked; the answer below builds on the four verified dimensions plus the repo's own first-hand inspection of three real Crestron packages (`/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/findings/03-crestron-package-format.md`, extracted at `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/tools/out/crestron/`) and a handful of checks I ran today against those files and the public NuGet feed. Where a fact comes from today's checks rather than the dossier, I say so.

## 1. The answer

Yes, with one large asterisk and one decisive test still to run. Reading Crestron drivers in is a clear yes, and cheaper than the doc-based research suggested: Crestron's own certified drivers turn out to be a plain JSON description of the device protocol (command templates, checksum rules, response decoders, polling policy) wrapped in a 16 KB generic .NET shell, and that JSON already lifts straight out of the package with a script. Writing Crestron drivers out is more plausible than the dossier concluded, for the same reason: the target is that JSON plus a ten-line shell, not hand-written C#, and the compiler and packaging tool are on public NuGet. The asterisk is that the SDK's license only permits use by parties holding a Crestron dealer, programmer or partner agreement, and the JSON-driver path Crestron uses for itself is not documented as a third-party authoring route. The decisive test is whether an unsigned, self-built package of that kind actually loads on a 4-Series processor; the documentation says third-party packages load without any signing, but nobody has proven it for this particular construction, and there is no Crestron hardware in evidence here. So: "in" yes, build it; "out" probably yes, but do not build it until one afternoon with a processor proves the load, and until the licensing position is settled. Everything else Crestron calls a "module" (SIMPL+, SIMPL#, user macros) is the wrong target and not worth the effort.

## 2. What a Crestron "module" actually is

The word covers five unrelated artifacts, and picking the right one is most of the answer. A SIMPL Windows user module (`.umc`) is a block of wiring in a graphical dataflow program; it has no named commands, only numbered digital/analog/serial "joins" (https://docs.crestron.com/en-us/Glossary/Content/Topics/Silos/Programming.htm). A SIMPL+ module (`.usp`) is a C-like text file that also exposes itself as joins; it compiles only inside SIMPL Windows, which is dealer-gated software, and community consensus (unverified against the official reference) is that it has no regular expressions. A SIMPL# library (`.clz`) is compiled C# with no source in the package; SIMPL# Pro (`.cpz`) is a whole control program, not a device module at all. None of these looks like an Extron ControlScript module.

The one that does is the Crestron Certified Driver package (`.pkg`). It is a plain ZIP that Crestron's own docs tell you to rename and open (https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/sdk/Crestron_Certified_Drivers_SDK/Content/Topics/Test-a-Driver/SIMPL-Testing/Load-Project.htm). It is not imported into a program; it is uploaded to the processor and loaded at run time by a generic per-category wrapper symbol in SIMPL, or dropped into Crestron Home's import folder (https://docs.crestron.com/en-us/8525/Content/CP4R/Appendix/Third-Party-Drivers/Load-Crestron-Drivers.htm), or consumed by .AV Framework and XiO Cloud. Inside the `.pkg` there are, in turn, three ways a driver can be written: the V1 "RAD" way (JSON metadata plus a compiled C# protocol class, https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/sdk/Crestron_Certified_Drivers_SDK/Content/Topics/Driver-SDK-V1/API-Reference/Device-Type-Abstract-Classes/ADeviceTypeProtocol.htm), the V2 "Entity Model" way (C# methods decorated with `[EntityCommand]`, whose bodies still send the bytes by hand, https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/sdk/Crestron_Certified_Drivers_SDK/Content/Topics/Driver-SDK-V2/Create-a-Driver/Add-Commands-and-Properties.htm), and a third way the tutorials never mention but the samples reveal: a `DriverDefinition` JSON document interpreted by Crestron's runtime engine, with the DLL reduced to a shell.

That third form is the target. The three Samsung packages in the repo show it directly. The Serial and IP DLLs are, byte for byte apart from the driver name, the same 16 KB shell: one class inheriting `Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core.LegacyWrappers.DisplayWrapperSerial` (or `DisplayWrapperTcp`), one `typeof()` call, and the driver JSON as an embedded resource. The IR package has no DLL at all, just a learned-code `.ir` file, a manifest and a PDF. The JSON's sections (`Commands`, `Responses`, `Transformations`, `Conditions`, `Rules`, `Controllers`, `Transports`, `InputOutput`, `SupportedFeatures`) match property-for-property the `DriverDefinition` class in Crestron's public API reference (https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/downloads/crestroncertifieddriversapi/html/Properties_T_Crestron_DeviceDrivers_SDK_DriverDefinition.htm), and the engine's loader, `DriverDefinitionInitialization`, is public too (https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/downloads/crestroncertifieddriversapi/html/T_Crestron_DeviceDrivers_SDK_DriverDefinitionInitialization.htm). The wrapper classes ship in the public DevKit's `Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core.dll` (Display, AVR, Cable Box, Video Server and a generic Capability wrapper, each in Serial/TCP/CEC flavours) but carry zero documentation comments. So the format is real, public in the runtime and the API reference, and undocumented as a thing you are invited to author. Its very name, "LegacyWrappers", is a warning that Crestron may be migrating away from it.

## 3. Crestron-IN

Verdict: feasible now for the drivers that matter most. For any package built the JSON-engine way (both non-IR Samsung packages, dated 2025, are), everything is recoverable: the wire bytes as composable templates with checksum and byte-conversion transformations, the response decoders (a tree of `Regex`, `BinaryPacket`, `Json` and name-match nodes), the per-feature polling interval, ack/feedback requirements, hold-off and retry counts, warm-up and cool-down timers, the input/output connector list, model lists, and the transport with its timing. The repo's finding that Extron's ControlScript and Crestron's JSON produce identical bytes for the same Samsung command (`self.build(0x01,0x00,0x00,value)` versus `"{:hex} 01 00 00 {Volume}"` inside a `08 22` packet with checksum) is the proof that this data can populate an Extron command table directly, and the Extron module's four binary `AddMatchString` patterns have exact counterparts in the Crestron decoder tree.

What is trapped: drivers written the V1 or V2 C# way, which is what the public tutorials teach third parties and what older Crestron drivers may be. There the outer `.dat` manifest still yields identity, transport defaults, model list and a feature checklist, but the protocol logic is compiled IL. Decompiling it is technically trivial (plain .NET, no obfuscation seen) and legally unattractive: the SDK license forbids reverse-engineering the SDK, and the terms covering downloaded drivers sit behind the portal login (https://drivers.crestron.io/) and were not read. Also trapped: password-protected `.usp`, any compiled `.ush`/`.uf`/`.clz`. An unprotected `.usp` is readable but is a join-wiring program, not a command table; recovering named commands from it is a heuristic exercise and I would not spend effort on that artifact class.

Two caveats for the Extron side of the pipe. The repo's finding 02 established that Extron's shipped runtime shell is SIS-specific (the `w0echo`/`Vrb3` handshake, the Extron error table), so a Crestron-derived third-party device needs the non-SIS ControlScript template, which the Samsung module already exemplifies. And there is no proof yet that every Crestron-authored driver uses the JSON engine (N=2 non-IR packages), which is why the sample list in section 7 matters.

## 4. Crestron-OUT

Verdict: plausible, unproven, and gated by licence and hardware rather than by code. The hardest blocker is not writing the driver, it is being allowed to build it and proving it loads. On building: the entire toolchain is on public NuGet with no login (`Crestron.DeviceDrivers.DevKit`, `ManifestUtil`, `ProgramInterface`, `Program`, all 27.0.24, owner Crestron_Electronics; checked today), the DevKit targets .NET Framework 4.7 and .NET 8, and `ManifestUtil` is a Windows `.exe` run automatically after build by an MSBuild target, producing the `.dat` and `.pkg`. But the bundled licence (Crestron "Software Development Tools License Agreement", 13 Feb 2024) states in §1.2 and §4.1(a) that you must be authorised under a separate written agreement (dealer, Authorized Independent Programmer, or partner), restricts use in §3.1 to developing software for Crestron devices, and forbids decompiling the tools in §4.2(c). Technically ungated, contractually gated.

On loading: the documented load path is upload via Toolbox File Manager or SFTP and reference by file path; no signature, certificate or approval step appears anywhere, and "certified" is purely a portal-listing status for Crestron-authored drivers (https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/sdk/Crestron_Certified_Drivers_SDK/Content/Topics/Submit-a-Driver/Submit-a-Driver.htm). The one in-the-wild failure report is a .NET version mismatch, not a trust error (https://www.reddit.com/r/crestron/comments/naxfxo/crestron_certified_display_driver_some_will_load/). Against that, I found today that Crestron's own driver DLLs are Authenticode-signed with a self-signed "Crestron Electronics / Firmware Department" certificate, and the wrapper path is undocumented, so nobody has shown that an unsigned shell built by an outsider loads. No verification code is visible in the SDK assemblies (only TLS certificate handling), which is consistent with "no gate", but that is an absence, not a proof. Testing requires a 4-Series processor or a Crestron Home processor plus Toolbox (dealer-gated). VC-4 runs .AV Framework, which imports drivers from the portal (https://docs.crestron.com/en-us/8275/Content/Topics/Setup.htm), but whether it accepts a side-loaded custom `.pkg` is unverified.

On the conversion itself: Extron's command table, parameter ranges and regexes map onto `Commands`, `Transformations`, `Controllers` and the `Regex`/`BinaryPacket` decoders well; the Samsung IP driver even handles HTTPS declaratively (`Secure: true`), which means the V1-documentation constraints the dossier flagged (one transport, TCP/HTTP only, HTTPS needs custom code at https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/sdk/Crestron_Certified_Drivers_SDK/Content/Topics/Driver-SDK-V1/API-Reference/Device-Type-Abstract-Classes/ATransportDriver.htm) apply to the C# authoring path, not to the engine. What does not map: Extron logic outside the auto-generated command block (conditional command construction, multi-step sequences) must be re-expressed in `Rules`/`Conditions` or dropped; the semantics of those sections are documented only at class-reference level and must be learned from samples; Crestron policy knobs such as feedback hold-off and retry count have no Extron source and need defaults; and on the SIMPL side the join surface is fixed by the generic wrapper symbol for the device category, so anything outside that category's vocabulary is invisible to a SIMPL programmer even if the JSON carries it. Extron devices with no clean category (Crestron has 21 native and 45 extension types, https://sdkcon78221.crestron.com/sdk/Crestron_Certified_Drivers_SDK/Content/Topics/Overview/Extension-Device-Categories.htm) need a judgement call per device.

## 5. Architecture: intermediate representation, shaped by the evidence

Firm recommendation: build a hub-and-spoke intermediate representation for the device-protocol layer, and model its concepts on Crestron's `DriverDefinition` (templates plus transformations for outgoing bytes, a decoder tree for incoming bytes, typed state controllers with polling policy, a transport block, a connector list), while keeping the Extron-to-Extron path as the AST-based source translator finding 02 already specified. The dossier, working from documentation alone, recommended point-to-point with a data sidecar because it believed Crestron's declarative layer stopped at a short whitelist of standard commands. The samples refute that for Crestron's own drivers: the whole protocol is data, and it is the most complete declarative device description either vendor ships. An IR with those concepts is one that a Crestron package fills nearly 1:1, that an Extron `.pkp` fills from its asset graph (`DriverCommandAsset`, `EnumStateAsset` wire tokens, `DecimalParamAsset` ranges) plus the delimited auto-generated block of its embedded Python, and that Control4's XML-plus-Lua and Q-SYS's Lua plugins would fit if they ever matter. Do not copy Crestron's JSON as the IR; emit it as one target.

The embedded-Python discovery does change the centre of gravity, in two opposite directions. For Extron-to-Extron it keeps the work in source translation, because the two dialects share most of their lines verbatim (finding 02; today's check on the Samsung pair: all four match-string regexes identical, 46% of the shipped module's non-blank lines present in the `.pkp` Python). For anything crossing to Crestron, the Python is the quarry, not the product: no Python survives the trip, only the protocol table lifted from it, and the `### BEGIN/END AUTO GENERATION` markers covering roughly three quarters of each embedded driver make that lifting mechanical. Hand-written Extron code outside the markers is the escape hatch and should be carried in the IR as an opaque, flagged node that the Crestron emitter reports as manual work, never silently dropped. The offline acceptance test is already available: regenerate the Samsung Crestron JSON from the Extron module and diff wire bytes per command against Crestron's own file.

## 6. Honest risks

Licensing is the largest. The DevKit is downloadable by anyone but licensed only to parties with an underlying Crestron agreement; building Crestron output without one is a contract breach even though nothing technical stops it. Reading Crestron packages needs no SDK, so Crestron-IN can be kept entirely outside those terms, but the driver files themselves come from a login-gated portal whose terms have not been read. On the Extron side the samples are Extron's copyrighted material and the repo is rightly private. Do not decompile `Core.dll` to learn rule semantics; learn them from samples and the public reference pages.

Format gating and fragility. The JSON-engine authoring path is undocumented, and its wrapper namespace is literally called "Legacy"; Crestron could drop or change it, whereas V1/V2 C# is the supported path. Crestron's own docs are internally inconsistent in places (the `GeneralInformation` page lists six device types where the categories page lists 21). The SIMPL+ reference and Crestron Home tutorials sit behind a JavaScript-rendered help site, and Toolbox and SIMPL Windows are dealer-gated (https://community.crestron.com/s/article/id-1000579, from the unverified dimension but consistent with the licence text).

Certification and signing. Certification is not required to load and is irrelevant to this tool; portal listing is optional with a two-week QE review. Signing is the open question above: Crestron signs its own DLLs with an internal certificate, third-party SDK drivers are documented to load unsigned, and the wrapper path has not been tested. Also note a per-driver `licenseRequired` flag exists in the manifest (false for Samsung), so some portal drivers are licence-locked.

Effort. Crestron-IN JSON extraction is essentially done (`/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json`); an IR importer plus an Extron non-SIS module generator is on the order of two to four weeks. Crestron-OUT is six to ten weeks after the licence and load questions are settled, needs a Windows build box for `ManifestUtil` (no `dotnet` or `mono` on this Mac), and only covers devices whose Extron logic lives in the declarative table. Prior art offers no shortcut: no cross-vendor driver converter exists anywhere, and the largest multi-platform driver house hand-ports (https://connectedmag.com.au/chowmain-driven-to-succeed/).

## 7. What to do next

First, settle the licence question, because it decides whether Crestron-OUT is even on the table: does Rob or his company hold a Crestron dealer, Authorized Independent Programmer or partner agreement, or can the work be done with a partner who does? If no, stop at Crestron-IN, which needs no SDK.

Second, get one afternoon with any 4-Series processor (or a Crestron Home CP4-R) and Toolbox, and run three loads in order: the unmodified Samsung Serial `.pkg` through the generic Display wrapper symbol as a baseline; a rebuild of that same driver from its extracted JSON with a hand-written ten-line `DisplayWrapperSerial` subclass, unsigned, built with the DevKit and `ManifestUtil`; then the same shell with JSON generated from the Extron Samsung module. If the second loads and behaves identically, Crestron-OUT is real; if it fails with a trust error, the JSON path is closed and only V1/V2 C# generation remains, which I would not pursue.

Third, obtain these files, in this order of value. Two or three more Crestron-authored `.pkg` files for devices Extron also covers, ideally one ASCII-protocol projector and one TCP device, to confirm the JSON engine is universal in Crestron's own output and to exercise the `Regex` decoders against Extron `AddMatchString` patterns. One third-party-authored `.pkg` from the portal, to learn whether the ingestible fraction of the portal is large or small. The portal's driver EULA text. The public API reference pages for `RuleDefinition`, `ControllerDefinition`, `ConditionType` and the `Transformations` namespace, scraped into a schema document alongside the samples. If IR control is in scope, an Extron IR driver and the `.ir` format notes, since the IR package has no DLL and is the cheapest full conversion of all. Skip SIMPL+ samples unless legacy `.usp` ingestion is a stated requirement.

Fourth, with no hardware needed, define the IR from the Samsung triple (the one device where `.pkp`, ControlScript and `.pkg` all exist), write the Crestron-JSON-to-IR importer and the Extron command-block-to-IR extractor, and make the offline wire-byte diff the acceptance test. That work is useful regardless of how the licence and load questions resolve.

## Bottom line up front

Three of the nine assigned dimensions — **artifact-landscape**, **modern-targets**, **direction-feasibility** — are empty test/placeholder payloads (`"summary": "test"`, one fake claim sourced to `example.com`). That's not "thin coverage," it's **no coverage**. And they're not minor dimensions: artifact-landscape was supposed to be the master enumeration of Crestron artifact types and name the single best analogue to Extron's ControlScript module; direction-feasibility was supposed to deliver the actual feasible/partial/no verdict per direction; modern-targets was supposed to say which Crestron target (CCD V1, V2, SIMPL, Crestron Home, .AV Framework) is even still current. **None of that exists.** Any verdict rendered today is being rendered on 6 of 9 legs. Say that to the owner plainly before anything else.

## What remains unanswered

- **Which Crestron target format the tool should actually aim at.** Six live dimensions each independently stumbled into pieces of "V1 vs V2 vs SIMPL+ vs Crestron Home vs Extension driver," but no dimension was tasked with reconciling them into one recommendation, and the one dimension whose job that was (modern-targets) is blank.
- **Whether an unsigned, self-built `.pkg` actually loads on real hardware.** This is the single load-bearing claim for the whole feasibility case ("no cryptographic gate found") and it rests entirely on the *absence* of a signing step being mentioned in one Crestron help page — nobody has built a `.pkg` and put it on a processor.
- **Whether the SDK's terms of use permit what this project wants to do at all**, independent of technical gating. Control4's SDK page was checked and found to auto-vest derivative works in Snap One. Nobody checked whether Crestron's Driver SDK EULA has an equivalent (or worse) clause. This could kill the project on paper regardless of technical feasibility, and it was never looked at.
- **Whether V2 "Entity Model" still ships a JSON manifest inside the `.pkg`, or whether metadata is purely reflected from compiled-DLL attributes at load time.** Flagged as open in ir-architecture, never resolved, yet it's central to whether V2 is "more declarative" than V1.
- **What a real `.pkg`'s file listing actually looks like** — root-level names, whether the DLL sits at archive root or a subfolder, whether the JSON/PDF/DLL filenames genuinely must match. Every dimension that touches this cites the *same* one Crestron doc page describing how to inspect it, not an actual inspection.
- **Whether SIMPL+ genuinely lacks regex.** The entire claim rests on a forum thread *title* ("Regular Expressions & Simpl+"), explicitly flagged by the researcher as unconfirmed against the real Language Reference Guide, which could not be fetched.
- **Testing without owning real hardware** (VirtualControl, simulators, Toolbox-only workflows) — never investigated at all; this was explicitly the direction-feasibility dimension's job and it's blank.

## Claims that survived only because nobody could check them

- **"No signing/certification gate exists in the load path."** Absence-of-mention in docs, not a test. Presented in ccd-package's summary as "the single most consequential finding for the project's viability" — that's a lot of weight on a negative inference.
- **"SIMPL+ has no regex."** Sourced to a forum thread title, not the language spec.
- **Chowmain's 2017 interview quote** ("some things we can do on one system can't be done on the other") is stretched into "the industry has not solved cross-format conversion." Two sentences from one founder, seven years old, generalized to the whole industry.
- **IEC TR 62795 as "the closest standardized precedent."** Verification caught that this standard was **withdrawn in 2017** — a fact sitting on the very page cited — and the original researcher didn't notice. A dead standard is now doing rhetorical work as "the precedent that exists."
- **The Jandy AquaLink `.clz` example ("plain, decompilable .NET assembly, not obfuscated")** is a single anecdote from one forum post, generalized into "the .clz format is not obfuscated."
- **"SIMPL Wrapper Module auto-generates a join-based front end from a typed driver's JSON"** (ccd-package finding 6, semantic-gap finding 6) — verification found the actual mechanism is the opposite: a small number of *generic, prebuilt* symbols per device-type category that any matching `.pkg` plugs into via a file-path string. The join surface is **shared and fixed per category**, not derived from that driver's own JSON. This is a materially different (more rigid) fact than what two dimensions built conclusions on, and the correction was never propagated back into their summaries.
- **Ultamation's "SIMPL Home" as evidence that even intra-Crestron bridging needs bespoke engineering** — refuted by verification, which found Crestron's own official, documented "Crestron Home SIMPL Integration Modules" bridge that the researcher never found. - **drivers.crestron.io** — login wall. Every dimension that needed a real `.pkg` sample hit this same gate independently (ccd-package, semantic-gap, ir-architecture, prior-art). This is the single most-cited gate in the whole dossier and it was never gotten around once.

`.smw`, `.umc`, `.cmc`, `.usp` (one real unencrypted community example was read — good — but no *password-protected* example), `.ush`/`.uf`, `.clz` (one third-party unzip anecdote, not directly inspected), `.cpz`, `.spz`/`.lpz`, `.vtp`/`.vtz`, `.c3p`, XiO Cloud driver format, `.AV Framework` driver format, Crestron Home Extension driver's actual on-disk format (is it `.pkg`? 2. **Transport model: HTTPS custom-only vs. prebuilt `HttpsTransport`.** ccd-package/semantic-gap cite `ATransportDriver.htm` saying HTTPS/SSH/WSS "must be implemented by the driver with its own custom transport class." semantic-gap's own verification found a sibling tutorial page in the same doc corpus naming a prebuilt `HttpsTransport` class in the same context. Crestron's own docs disagree with each other here, and nobody resolved it.
3. **Device-type taxonomy size disagrees across Crestron's own pages, and two different dimensions hit this independently without cross-referencing.** ir-architecture's verification found `GeneralInformation.htm`'s `DeviceType` enum lists only 6 values while `Extension-Device-Categories.htm` lists 20+ "Native" plus ~40 "Extension" types. semantic-gap's verification separately caught a Native-vs-Extension mislabeling on the same category page. Three dimensions (ccd-package, semantic-gap, ir-architecture) each treat "the taxonomy" as a stable input to their conclusions; it isn't stable even within Crestron's own docs.
4. **prior-art's "even intra-Crestron bridging is hard" thesis vs. the (missed, then found-by-verification) official Crestron Home↔SIMPL bridge.** The original finding used Ultamation's paid product as evidence of difficulty; verification found Crestron ships an official, documented bridge mechanism the product sits on top of. This undercuts a claim other dimensions lean on rhetorically (that Crestron's own ecosystem is already fragmented beyond easy bridging).
